title: Resolving Forward and Backward Jump Labels in a Two-Pass Assembler
description: See why forward jump references require a symbol-table pass before emitting instructions, while backward references resolve in one pass.
source: draft: agy free model + edit: codex

steps.description: `SOURCE` (lines 8-14) contains five assembly instructions with two labels: `start:` at the top and `done:` at the bottom. Its two jumps are `JMPZ x done` on line 10 and `JMPZ x start` on line 12. `split_label` separates an optional `label:` prefix from the instruction text.
`pass1(source)` walks every line without emitting instructions: it increments `address` for each instruction (line 31) and records `labels[label] = address` whenever a label appears (line 29).

`pass2(source, labels)` walks `source` a second time with the completed `labels` dictionary in hand. Whenever `parts[0] == "JMPZ"` on line 42, line 43 replaces the target name `parts[2]` with `str(labels[parts[2]])`.

steps.question: In the single-pass loop on lines 61-80, `seen` only records labels encountered so far. Which of the two `JMPZ` instructions (`JMPZ x done` at address 1 or `JMPZ x start` at address 3) resolves, and which prints `???`?
steps.answer: At address 1, `JMPZ x done` prints `???`. `done:` is a forward reference at address 4 that has not been reached yet. At address 3, `JMPZ x start` resolves to `0` because `start:` was already recorded in `seen` at address 0.

steps.description: Lines 61-80 run the single-pass attempt. `target in seen` on line 71 fails for the forward jump to `'done'` at address 1. It succeeds for the backward jump to `'start'` at address 3.
Inside `pass2`, line 43 looks up `labels['done']` (`4`) and rewrites `JMPZ x done` at address 1 into `JMPZ x 4`.
